study-intro-p1: Thank you for participating in this study. We are researchers interested in how people write professional emails in everyday workplace situations.
study-intro-p2: Your responses are completely voluntary and will be kept confidential. You may withdraw at any time without penalty.
study-phase-1-desc: Write an email on your own
study-phase-2-desc: Write an email with AI assistance
study-phase-3-desc: Write an email with AI assistance
study-instruct-header: A few things to keep in mind
study-instruct-1: There are no right or wrong answers. We are interested in how you would naturally write.
study-instruct-2: Please write the email as if you were actually going to send it.
study-instruct-4: Do not worry about grammar or spelling — content matters more.
study-before-begin-header: About your supervisor in this study
study-before-begin-p1-intro: In each task, we would like you to imagine the following situation:
study-before-begin-p1-bold: you have recently started a new job and have met your supervisor only once. You do not yet know them well. Your supervisor is currently away from the office and has asked to be contacted by email only for now.
study-before-begin-incentive-body-intro: At the end of the study, you will receive personalized feedback on your communication style based on the emails you write.
study-before-begin-incentive-body-bold: To make this feedback meaningful, please write each email as naturally as you would in that situation.
study-scenario-1a: You have a report due this Friday. Yesterday you discovered a major error in the data analysis that requires you to redo a significant portion of the work. You estimate you need two extra days. The report is scheduled to be delivered to a client on Friday, and the client is relying on it to prepare for an important presentation on Monday. If you need an extension, your boss will have to contact the client directly to explain the delay. Without the extension, the report will be incomplete and potentially inaccurate.
study-scenario-1a-task: Write an email to your boss asking for a deadline extension.
study-scenario-1b: You are applying for a competitive industry award that recognizes early-career professionals. The application deadline is in two weeks, and a recommendation letter from a direct supervisor is required. You have not yet asked your boss, and you are aware they have a very busy schedule this month due to an ongoing client project.
study-scenario-1b-task: Write an email to your boss asking them to write you a recommendation letter for the award.
study-scenario-1c: A close friend is getting married this Saturday. You need to travel out of town from Thursday evening through Sunday — effectively three working days away. You only found out last week that you are needed as part of the wedding party, so the request is coming on very short notice. Your boss has a known policy of not approving last-minute leave requests, and similar requests from colleagues have been turned down in the past. Missing your close friend's wedding is not an option for you.
study-scenario-1c-task: Write an email to your boss requesting three days of leave this week.
study-scenario-2a: In today's team meeting, your boss outlined a plan to switch to a different data collection method midway through the current project. Based on your experience with the previous phase, you believe this change will introduce inconsistencies in the dataset that will make the final analysis unreliable. If the project proceeds this way, the results may not hold up to scrutiny when presented to stakeholders.
study-scenario-2a-task: Write an email to your boss expressing your concern about this direction.
study-scenario-2b: Yesterday your boss returned your draft report with a comment saying your sales figures for Q3 were "significantly overstated" and asked you to revise them downward. However, you have double-checked the original data source and confirmed that your numbers are accurate. Changing the figures as requested would introduce incorrect information that could mislead the team's planning decisions.
study-scenario-2b-task: Write an email to your boss explaining that you believe the figures are correct.
study-scenario-2c: In this morning's team meeting, your boss announced a decision to move up the product launch date by four weeks. You are responsible for quality testing, and you know that at the current pace, testing will not be complete by the new date. Launching with untested features risks customer-facing bugs that could damage the company's reputation and require costly emergency fixes after launch.
study-scenario-2c-task: Write an email to your boss expressing your concern about the revised launch timeline.
study-scenario-3a: Your boss has just asked you to lead a new client proposal that needs to be submitted by end of next week. You are currently managing two ongoing projects, both with critical deadlines within the next ten days. Taking on the proposal would require approximately 15 additional hours of work, meaning you would not be able to meet your existing deadlines without serious quality trade-offs.
study-scenario-3a-task: Write an email to your boss explaining that you are not able to take on the new project at this time.
study-scenario-3b: It is Thursday afternoon, and your boss has just asked you to come in this Saturday to finalize a presentation for a Monday client meeting. You already have a non-negotiable family commitment this weekend — your parents are visiting from out of town for the first time in over a year, and the plans were made months ago. Missing this would disappoint your family and cannot be rescheduled.
study-scenario-3b-task: Write an email to your boss explaining that you are not able to come in this weekend.
study-scenario-3c: Your boss has just asked you to give a 20-minute presentation tomorrow afternoon on the new system your team has been developing. The audience will include senior leadership. You were only informed today and have not had time to prepare slides or organize your talking points. Presenting without adequate preparation risks giving inaccurate information to senior leadership and could reflect poorly on both you and your team.
study-scenario-3c-task: Write an email to your boss explaining that you do not feel prepared to present tomorrow.

study-before-ai-p1: For the next two tasks, you will write about the same situation again — this time with the help of an AI writing assistant.
study-before-ai-bullet-1: You can ask the AI to draft the email for you.
study-before-ai-bullet-2: You are free to edit the draft generated by the AI in any way you like.
study-before-ai-bullet-3: The final email you submit is what matters — write it in whatever way feels right to you.
study-email-body-placeholder-2: Write your email here, or click Generate Draft above…

study-task-design-note: Make sure you write the email in ways that you feel comfortable sending to your boss.
study-pref-header: Which AI draft felt more natural?
study-pref-p1: Looking back at the two AI-generated drafts you received — one in Task 2 and one in Task 3 — which felt more natural or appropriate for the situation?

study-results-p1: Thank you for participating in this study. Your responses have been recorded.
study-results-profile-low-desc: Your email tended toward direct, low-context communication. You stated your point clearly without relying heavily on implicit cues or softening devices. This style is valued for its clarity and is common in many Western professional environments.
study-results-profile-balanced-desc: Your email showed a blend of direct and indirect communication. You balanced clarity with some softening devices or hedging, reflecting an adaptive style that draws from both low- and high-context approaches.
study-results-profile-high-desc: Your email tended toward contextual, high-context communication. You used indirect language and politeness markers, relying on context and tone to convey your message. This style emphasizes relationship preservation and is common in many East Asian professional environments.
study-results-cultural-low: This pattern is more common in Western professional contexts, where directness and clarity are valued.
study-results-cultural-balanced: This pattern blends traits found in both Western and East Asian professional contexts.
study-results-cultural-high: This pattern is more common in East Asian professional contexts, where indirectness and relational sensitivity are valued.
study-results-feedback-note: This analysis is based on linguistic patterns in your email and is for educational purposes only. It does not reflect a judgment of your communication skills.
study-results-contact: If you have any questions about this study, please contact the research team at shinsaka@iu.edu.
litw-irb2-header: Before we get started, here are a few things you should know...
litw-irb2-q1: What is this study all about?
litw-irb2-a1-p1: In this study, you will be asked to write professional emails in a series of workplace scenarios. We are interested in how people communicate in professional settings.
litw-irb2-q2: What data are we going to collect?
litw-irb2-a2: We will collect the emails you write during the study, along with basic demographic information. We will not collect your name or contact information. Your data will be stored securely and used only for research purposes.
litw-irb2-q3: Do I have to be in this study?
litw-irb2-a3: No, participation is entirely voluntary. You can stop at any time without penalty.
litw-irb2-q4: Who can you contact if you have questions?
litw-irb2-a4-p1: If you have questions, please contact the research team at shinsaka@iu.edu.
litw-irb2-a4-p2: If you want to talk about the study with someone who is not part of the study team, contact the Indiana University IRB at irb@iu.edu.
